address_spaces.name: I/O
address_spaces.notes: Sixteen small windows of 16 MB fill offsets 0x0000_0000 to 0x0fff_ffff, widget N at N times 16 MB. Seven big windows of 512 MB start at 0x2000_0000. Small window 0 and big window 6 are two views of the same widget, and both decode: Linux reads widget 0's identification register through the small window by its raw address, OpenBSD reaches the same device through the big window, so both paths have to work. See docs/datasheets/address-map.md for the small-window-0 reversal history.

buses.name: Bridge one-wire line
buses.notes:
**A different bus from the IOC3's MicroLAN**, and the distinction is load-bearing. The Bridge has its own one-wire master at widget offset 0x00_00b0, driven a bit at a time — bit 0 samples the wire, bit 1 says the slot finished, a write starts a slot with its low-drive and remaining times packed in. Linux and OpenBSD read the layout the same way, but their timings differ slightly, so a model must key off the sequence of slots rather than exact microseconds.
**Mainline Linux will not boot without it.** It reads the board-identity NIC before doing anything else with the Bridge, and a failed read makes the driver return a deferred-probe error so the Bridge never attaches — no PCI bus, no I/O controller, no console, no disk, and a deferred-probe message as the only clue.
sources: docs/datasheets/bridge.md lines 731-745, citing Linux mainline commit db2ddb87143519e20a95aa36c60b36107b736a58, establishes the Bridge one-wire master

buses.name: Hub one-wire line
buses.notes: The Hub memory/directory interface owns this third one-wire master. The hardware endpoint is a DS2505-compatible responder whose pages describe the installed PIMM population, part number, installed revision, and barcode serial. The current model implements an empty bus. The responder's package, reference designator, connector contact, and copper route remain unresolved.

regions.name: console port
regions.notes: Measured from the chip's own register block, not from an address space — computing an absolute address by adding this to a space base gives a number that means nothing. The chip's serial block sits in a window at 0x20000 and port A is at 0x178 inside it, so 0x20178 is the offset that reaches the port's first 16550 register. Its low twelve bits, 0x178, are separately what a guest reads to decide which controller generation this is; at or above 0x380 it would read a configuration register that does not exist here. Two facts, two masks, one number.

views.name: reset vector view
views.notes: Where the processor's reset vector reaches it. The reset vector 0xffff_ffff_bfc0_0000 lands in the **uncached** compatibility segment at 0xffff_ffff_a000_0000, not the cached one at 0xffff_ffff_8000_0000 — the cached segment is what the guests read the firmware parameter block through. The two behave differently and the distinction has cost this team a week once already.

views.name: Hub special view
views.notes: One region aliased into both views. Which bus the flash hangs off is settled — the memory and directory unit — and that also explains the part that looked odd: the reset vector reaches the flash in uncached *memory* space rather than through an I/O space because memory space is what that unit decodes, so the flash sits inside it rather than beside it. What remains open is narrower: how a compatibility-segment access physically resolves to flash rather than to memory at the same offset, traced in the compatibility-segment routing note, whose source reading is settled and three-sourced but whose hardware implication is contradicted by real-hardware evidence. The alias gives every guest what it expects meanwhile.

views.name: remote Hub special view
views.notes: Node-explicit maintenance view of the same flash storage.

components.description: Battery-backed non-volatile memory with a real-time clock, on the IOC3's byte bus.
components.name: MK48T35-class Timekeeper
components.notes: Byte-bus chip select 0 is what makes this a Timekeeper. Chip selects 1 and 2 mean a DS1687 instead, which is the Octane's clock and is indirectly addressed. The two are not interchangeable. The provenance is SGI's own clock driver for this generation rather than a guest's, and the distinction was worth making: mainline Linux does carry a driver for this part, but its build condition names no SGI machine at all, so citing it would have been a fact about a driver that exists rather than about this board. The public header that does name this board defines its subsystem identifier and says nothing about a clock.

aliases: one-wire family code 0x0b — how Linux recognises it on this master
components.description: The board-identity NIC reached through the Bridge's own one-wire master. Its physical attachment within the Origin 200 assembly is not established.
components.name: board-identity NIC
components.notes: What must be on the far side is specific: Linux looks for family code 0x0b on this master and ignores anything else, then reads the first 64 bytes as two independent 32-byte blocks, each with an inverted CRC-16 in its last two bytes so a CRC over the whole block leaves a fixed residue. Both blocks must check out or the memory is treated as unreadable. Existence and contents are observed: a real Origin 200 printed this board's identity string. Placement behind the Bridge one-wire master is derived by pairing that observation with the cited public Linux driver, not claimed as part of the hardware capture.

components.description: The Origin 200's instance of the SN0 Module System Controller (MSC; "ELSC" is SGI's own older name for the same part): a separate board answering as a slave on the I2C bus the PCF8584 masters. It takes a checksummed ASCII command and response protocol covering power control, reset and switch readback on the Origin 200 (the family protocol also carries an 8-character display and multi-module commands the Origin 200 has no hardware for), and separately multiplexes a serial terminal on its own rear diagnostic connector onto the same link.
components.name: ELSC
components.notes: This one is attested by our own machine's manual rather than a neighbour's: the Origin 200 Owner's Guide documents reaching the controller with a control-T escape and gives its prompt. The Origin 2000 and Onyx2 carry a different controller with a keyswitch, an eight-character display and eight debug switches, and none of that describes this part.
sources: 007-3708-002 Origin 200 and Origin 200 GIGAchannel Owner's Guide, printed page 123

aliases: NVRAM (the firmware's own term for it)
components.description: A serial non-volatile store answering as a slave on the same I2C bus the system controller sits on. It holds the module, partition, domain, cluster and cell numbers, the supervisor password, the debug-switch values and the built-in-self-test flag.
components.name: I2C configuration NVRAM
components.notes: NOT the same part as the machine's other non-volatile store: the clock component is a battery-backed Timekeeper on the I/O controller's BYTE BUS at chip select 0, and this is a separate device on the HUB'S I2C BUS, reached by raw transactions the system controller never sees. The distinction's history is in the pcf8584-elsc datasheet's behavioral notes. It answers EIGHT CONSECUTIVE SLAVE ADDRESSES FROM 0x50, the top three bits of an eleven-bit byte address choosing among them and the low byte addressing within one. Whether that is one 2 KB part consuming eight addresses or several smaller ones is not established, and the firmware cannot tell either. The system controller's own reserved area is the last of the eight, which SGI's PROM Technical Reference corroborates independently by reserving the top 256 bytes for the controller's use. The `kind` is the least-wrong available value: this is an EEPROM rather than flash, and what the field is carrying here is the role of non-volatile storage.

components.description: A single-byte read and write target answering on the Hub's I2C bus at slave address 0x20, driven directly by a pair of firmware routines the interactive monitor calls.
components.name: Unidentified I2C device at slave address 0x20
components.notes: WHAT THIS DEVICE IS HAS NOT BEEN ESTABLISHED, and the reviewed datasheet deliberately declines to guess. The entry exists because an unidentified part that provably answers is inventory: a model implementing only the system controller leaves this address unanswered, and leaving the entry out because the part cannot be named is the omission a completeness audit exists to surface rather than a reason to stay silent. The `kind` is a PLACEHOLDER and should not be read as a claim -- the enum has no value for an unidentified device, and nothing establishes that this one is storage. What would settle it is a firmware routine read for what it does with the byte, or a board document naming a part at this address.

machine.notes: The one-module GIGAchannel system: the two-CPU, 128 MiB attached module from the upgrade guide with its cabinet. A cabinet may attach to either module of a two-module system, but one cabinet cannot be shared between modules and cabinets cannot be daisy-chained; this configuration builds the one-module form only.

space_selection.notes: Two bits the processor drives beside the address, not part of it. All four spaces decode to the same 40-bit physical address and the attribute is what tells them apart. Emulator carrier addresses are target implementation metadata and do not belong in this shared hardware layer.
